messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas Avery was seventy-eight when he was hospitalized with a sudden, life-threatening illness that began at home and ended in the intensive care unit. He had been a meticulous database administrator for years, still working part-time from a home office after most men his age had retired, and he was used to trusting systems that behaved predictably. The illness shattered that assumption. He remembered the speed with which his body failed him: the shortness of breath, the confusion, the humiliating dependence on strangers moving quickly around his bed while machines alarmed and oxygen hissed beside him. What remained with him most powerfully was not a coherent story but sensory fragments. Even months later, when the memory came, he could smell the sharp antiseptic and the plastic, medical odor of tubing and oxygen. In those moments he did not feel as if he were recalling something from the past; he felt as though he were back in that hospital bed, with the scene more vivid and immediate than ordinary memory, as if it were happening again in the present.

After he was discharged, Thomas expected gratitude and relief. Instead he found himself unsettled by how little safety meant to him now. He could be sitting in his own living room and still feel on guard, listening to his breathing, noticing every flutter in his chest, every shift in his stomach. At home, where he had once felt most at ease, he began scanning for signs that something catastrophic was about to happen again. The watchfulness had a grim logic for him. He had learned, as he saw it, that danger could come from inside his own body without warning. He was left with strong waves of fear and anger, and under them a hard bitterness that life itself had become unreliable.

The quality of his memories seemed to deepen these conclusions. When the smell of disinfectant or even a chemically clean scent drifted up while he was wiping down his desk or opening supplies in his home office, he could be pulled straight back into the worst moments of the illness. In those episodes, the memory felt more real than the room he was standing in. What frightened him most was what he took these experiences to mean. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his ally, that it kept reacting as if he were still in mortal danger because, in some essential way, the danger had never really passed. The vivid reliving did not feel like memory to him; it felt like proof. From there, his thinking darkened further. If his own body could turn on him so suddenly, then the world was not orderly or benevolent but fundamentally dangerous, and whatever faith he had once had in life’s fairness had eroded.

His constant state of alertness reinforced the same beliefs. Thomas found himself checking locks, checking his pulse, checking whether he could take a full breath, even when he knew rationally he was home and medically stable. He was superalert to noises in the apartment at night and equally watchful of sensations inside himself during the day. The more he lived in this keyed-up state, the more convinced he became that his system was warning him of something real. He was certain that if he let his guard down, he would miss the next sign and pay for it. That vigilance fed his sense that the world was dangerous and his body an enemy that might betray him again at any moment. The emotional toll was immediate: fear first, then anger, and sometimes a bleak, almost ashamed sense of how completely his confidence had collapsed.

These changes began to shape his daily life. Because he still managed databases remotely, his work should have offered routine, but even there he was not free of reminders. The sterile smell of packaged electronics, cleaning wipes on his keyboard, and the enclosed quiet of long hours at his desk could all sharpen his awareness of his body and leave him braced for disaster rather than absorbed in the task. He remained functional, but with increasing effort, and his world narrowed around the project of staying ready. As a divorced man living alone, there was no one present to interrupt the private logic that had taken hold.

By the time he sought help, Thomas was exhausted by living as though survival still depended on unbroken vigilance. He spoke less about the illness itself than about what it had done to his view of existence. He no longer trusted life, no longer trusted his body, and no longer felt truly safe even in his own home. What finally brought him in was the recognition that the memories were not fading and that his days were being organized around threat rather than work, rest, or pleasure. He said he wanted, more than anything, to feel that being alive did not have to mean being on guard every minute, but he was afraid that lowering his guard would be the moment something terrible happened again.
